title: How does consulting recruiting work, from application to offer?
description: The typical stages of consulting recruiting for students and experienced hires: applications, tests, interview rounds, timing and what each stage screens for.
hook: Consulting recruiting can feel like a maze of deadlines, tests and rounds. Once you see the overall shape, it is much less daunting, because most firms follow a similar pattern. Here it is.
body:
The usual stages

  1. Research and networking. Learning about firms and talking to people who work there. How to network.
  2. Application. CV, often a cover letter, sometimes transcripts. How to write a consulting CV.
  3. Online assessment. Game-based tests, chatbot cases, numerical tests or recorded video answers, depending on the firm. How to prepare.
  4. First-round interviews. Usually two interviews, each with a case and fit questions.
  5. Final round. Two or three interviews with senior people, sometimes with written or group cases.
  6. Offer. Often within days of the final round.

Students: timing matters

Many firms recruit students on an annual cycle, with deadlines for internships and graduate roles months before the start date. Internships are a common route to full-time offers. Check each firm's deadlines early, and note that dates differ by country and office.

Experienced hires

Recruiting is usually rolling rather than seasonal, often starts with a recruiter conversation, and may include interviews about your industry expertise as well as cases.

What each stage screens for

  • CV: academic strength, achievement and leadership.
  • Tests: problem solving and numeracy under time pressure.
  • Interviews: structured thinking, maths, communication, and whether you would be good with clients and colleagues.

Give yourself enough time

Most people need several weeks of steady case practice. The three-week plan is a good starting point once you have interviews booked.

An example timeline for a student (illustrative)

  • Months 1 to 2: research firms, attend events, talk to people, polish your CV.
  • Month 3: applications and online tests.
  • Months 3 to 4: first-round interviews, then final rounds, often a week or two apart.
  • Month 4: offers.

Actual dates differ by country, firm and whether you are applying for an internship or a full-time role, so build your own calendar from each firm's deadlines.

Sources

  • Hacking the Case Interview: BCG hiring process
  • IGotAnOffer: McKinsey interview process

Checked November 2026.

Make the recruiting funnel measurable

Treat applications as a funnel, not a verdict on your worth. Track firm and team, referral/contact, application date, assessment status, interview stage and next action. If you submit 30 well-targeted applications and receive only two initial calls, the problem to investigate is positioning or role fit before you spend another month doing case drills. If you consistently reach final rounds but no offer, collect detailed interview feedback and look for a repeated weakness.

Separate two parallel workstreams. The first is getting selected: a results-focused CV, appropriate role targeting, outreach and compelling motivation. The second is performing once selected: numerical fluency, case leadership, communication and fit stories. Doing twenty mock cases will not compensate for an application that never reaches an interviewer.

Check firm deadlines and programme eligibility before creating your plan; campus and experienced-hire routes can differ. Keep a versioned bank of application stories, but edit the proof points and motivations for each team. In interviews, be ready to explain why that particular work suits your background rather than listing brand prestige as the reason.
